name: Database basics
explanation: A database keeps related information together. A table holds one kind of record. In astronauts, each row describes one person and each column describes one attribute. SQL is the language we use to ask the database questions.
mistake: A row is one candidate. A column such as role describes every candidate.

name: SELECT · FROM
explanation: SELECT chooses what to display. FROM tells PostgreSQL which table to read. An asterisk means every column.
mistake: Spell the table name exactly. An asterisk belongs after SELECT.

name: Selecting columns
explanation: List the column names after SELECT in the order you want to read them. Separate each name with a comma.
mistake: A comma goes between columns. A trailing comma before FROM is unnecessary.

name: DISTINCT
explanation: DISTINCT keeps one copy of each combination of values in the selected columns. Selecting a unique ID as well would keep every astronaut.
mistake: DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row. Choose only the columns you want to deduplicate.

name: WHERE
explanation: WHERE tests each record. A row appears only when the condition is true. Surround text values with single quotes.
mistake: Use 'Pilot' for text. Double quotes identify a column or table in PostgreSQL.

name: Comparison operators
explanation: Use = for equal, <> or != for different, < and > for strict limits, and <= or >= to include the boundary. Experience is measured in years.
syntax: SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE number_column >= number;
example: SELECT name FROM astronauts WHERE experience < 5;
mistake: At least includes the number itself. A strict > would drop candidates at the boundary.

name: AND
explanation: AND requires both conditions to hold on the same row. Add another AND to require a third condition. Boolean values TRUE and FALSE can be written without quotes.
syntax: SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE condition_a AND condition_b;
example: SELECT * FROM astronauts WHERE role = 'Pilot' AND available = TRUE;
mistake: Every condition needs its own comparison or Boolean expression.

name: OR
explanation: OR accepts a row when at least one of its conditions is true. Repeat the column comparison on each side.
syntax: SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE condition_a OR condition_b;
example: SELECT name FROM astronauts WHERE role = 'Pilot' OR role = 'Engineer';
mistake: Writing role = 'Pilot' OR 'Doctor' leaves the second condition incomplete.

name: NOT
explanation: NOT reverses a condition. Parentheses make the scope clear. With non-null values, NOT (a = b) and a <> b select the same rows.
example: SELECT name FROM astronauts WHERE NOT (available = TRUE);
mistake: NOT around a whole pair of conditions reverses the pair. Use parentheses to show your intention.

name: Combined conditions
explanation: Build your filter one condition at a time. PostgreSQL evaluates NOT before AND, then OR. Group alternatives in parentheses when a restriction applies to both.
syntax: SELECT a, b FROM table_name WHERE (test_a OR test_b) AND test_c;
example: SELECT name FROM astronauts WHERE (role = 'Pilot' OR role = 'Doctor') AND available;
mistake: Check the requested columns, availability, clearance and the experience boundary separately.
